content: Write a letter of recommendation for an employee applying for an internal promotion.

**[Company Name / Letterhead]**
[Street Address]
[City, State ZIP]

[Date]

[Recipient Name]
[Recipient Title]
[Department]
[Company Name]

**Re: Recommendation for [Employee Name] — [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Mr./Ms./Dr. Last Name or Hiring Committee],

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for [Employee Name]'s promotion to [Target Position Title]. I have had the pleasure of working with [Employee First Name] for [number] years as [his/her/their] [direct manager / team lead / cross-functional partner] in the [Department] group, and in that time [he/she/they] [has/have] consistently performed at a level that exceeds the expectations of [his/her/their] current role. In my view, this promotion would formalize responsibilities [Employee First Name] has already begun to shoulder.

[Employee First Name] joined our team in [Month, Year] as a [Current Title], and the trajectory since has been remarkable. Among [his/her/their] most significant contributions:

- **[Achievement 1]** — [e.g., Led the migration of our client onboarding process to the new platform, reducing average onboarding time from 14 days to 5 and eliminating roughly 200 hours of manual work per quarter.]
- **[Achievement 2]** — [e.g., Owned the quarterly forecasting model, improving accuracy from ±12% to ±4% and giving leadership meaningfully better visibility into pipeline risk.]
- **[Achievement 3]** — [e.g., Mentored three junior analysts, two of whom have since been promoted, and built the training documentation now used department-wide.]

Beyond results, what distinguishes [Employee First Name] is [his/her/their] judgment. [He/She/They] [is/are] the person colleagues seek out when a problem is ambiguous, because [he/she/they] ask[s] the right questions before proposing solutions and [is/are] candid about tradeoffs rather than telling people what they want to hear. During [specific challenging period or project — e.g., the Q3 vendor transition], [he/she/they] kept a stressed cross-functional team aligned and communicated proactively with stakeholders at every level, including [senior leader or client name/type].

The [Target Position Title] role calls for [key requirement 1, e.g., managing a team of five] and [key requirement 2, e.g., owning the departmental budget]. [Employee First Name] has already demonstrated capability in both areas: [brief evidence, e.g., informally leading a three-person workstream since January and co-managing a $1.2M project budget without a single overrun]. I am confident [he/she/they] would step into the expanded scope with a short ramp-up.

To be balanced, [Employee First Name] and I have discussed [growth area — e.g., delegating more readily rather than absorbing work personally], and [he/she/they] [has/have] made deliberate progress on it over the past [timeframe] — a sign of the coachability that makes me confident in [his/her/their] continued growth at the next level.

Losing [Employee First Name] from my team would be a real cost to our group, and I recommend [him/her/them] anyway, because [he/she/they] [has/have] earned this and the organization will be better for it. Please feel free to contact me at [phone] or [email] if I can provide further detail.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]
[Department] | [Company Name]
[Phone] | [Email]

---

**A few tips for adapting this:**
- **Quantify at least two accomplishments.** Numbers ("cut cycle time 40%") are far more persuasive than adjectives ("hardworking").
- **Map to the job description.** Pull two or three requirements from the posting and give direct evidence for each — internal committees screen for exactly this.
- **Include one honest growth area with evidence of improvement.** It makes the praise credible; pure superlatives read as boilerplate.
- **Address the "backfill" question if you're the current manager.** Signaling that you support the move despite the cost to your own team carries real weight.

If you share the employee's actual accomplishments and the role details, I'm happy to draft a fully specific version.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

**[Company Name / Letterhead]**

[Date]

**Re: [Employee Name] — Promotion to [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Name / Promotion Committee],

You know [Employee First Name]'s record, so I'll skip the summary and give you the part you can't get from the file: my assessment of whether [he/she/they] can do the job at the next level. [He/She/They] can, and I'd argue [he/she/they] already [is/are].

Three things I'd want weighed in the decision:

**1. [He/She/They] [has/have] been operating above grade for [timeframe].** The [project/workstream, e.g., vendor transition] was scoped as a [Current Title] deliverable and became something larger — [brief outcome, e.g., a full process redesign that cut cycle time 40% and is now the standard across three regions]. Nobody assigned that expansion; [Employee First Name] saw it and took it.

**2. The judgment holds up under pressure.** During [specific difficult episode], [he/she/they] [chose/pushed back/escalated] [specific decision] when the easier move was [alternative]. That call cost [him/her/them] [short-term friction/goodwill with X] and was correct. That's the behavior I most want in this seat, and it's the hardest thing to verify from a résumé.

**3. [He/She/They] build[s] capability in other people.** [Brief evidence — e.g., two of the three analysts [he/she/they] mentored have been promoted; the onboarding documentation [he/she/they] wrote is now used department-wide.] The current role doesn't reward this. The target role depends on it.

On the concern I expect will come up: [state it plainly — e.g., [he/she/they] [has/have] not formally managed direct reports / limited exposure to [X] stakeholders / relatively short tenure at grade]. It's fair, and I don't think it's disqualifying. [Evidence/mitigation — e.g., [he/she/they] [has/have] led a three-person workstream informally since January, including two difficult performance conversations [he/she/they] handled without my involvement.] The gap is experience, not aptitude, and it closes faster in the role than outside it.

One more thing worth saying explicitly: this promotion takes [Employee First Name] off my team, and I'm recommending it anyway. I'd rather absorb the backfill than watch [him/her/them] plateau here or take the growth somewhere else.

Happy to discuss candidly, on or off the record — [phone] / [email].

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

---

**What changed and why:**

| First version (reader is new to the candidate) | This version (reader knows the background) |
|---|---|
| Opens by establishing your relationship and tenure | Opens by naming what you're uniquely positioned to add |
| Recounts the career trajectory and hire date | Assumes it; goes straight to the above-grade evidence |
| Lists achievements broadly | Selects the two or three that specifically predict success at the *next* level |
| Maps the job description requirement by requirement | Assumes the committee has the JD; addresses the likely *objection* instead |
| Growth area framed gently as coachability | Growth area named plainly, because a knowledgeable reader will raise it anyway and pre-empting it builds credibility |
| Formal, complete, ~500 words | Compressed, conversational, argumentative — a memo between peers |

The core principle: with an informed reader, description is noise. Everything that survives the edit should be either **evidence they don't have** (private moments of judgment, unassigned work, difficult conversations you witnessed) or **an argument** about how to interpret evidence they do have.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

**Re: [Employee Name] — Promotion to [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Name / Promotion Committee],

Promote [Employee First Name]. [He/She/They] [has/have] been doing this job for [timeframe] without the title.

You have the record; here's what isn't in it. The [project/workstream] was scoped as a [Current Title] deliverable and [Employee First Name] expanded it into [outcome — e.g., a process redesign that cut cycle time 40%, now standard across three regions]. Nobody assigned that. During [difficult episode], [he/she/they] [specific decision] when the easier move was [alternative] — it cost [him/her/them] [short-term friction] and it was right. And [he/she/they] build[s] other people: [evidence — e.g., two of three analysts [he/she/they] mentored have since been promoted]. The current role doesn't reward that. This one requires it.

The likely objection — [state it, e.g., no formal direct reports] — is fair. [He/She/They] [has/have] led [scope] informally since [month], including [specific hard thing handled independently]. The gap is experience, not aptitude, and it closes faster in the seat than outside it.

This takes [Employee First Name] off my team and I'm recommending it anyway. I'd rather absorb the backfill than watch [him/her/them] plateau.

Happy to discuss candidly — [phone] / [email].

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

---

**What I cut:** the numbered structure and headers (unnecessary at this length), the framing sentences that announced what I was about to say, and one of the three evidence points' elaboration. The opening line now carries the recommendation, so a reader who stops after ten words still gets it.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

**Re: [Employee Name] — Promotion to [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Name / Promotion Committee],

Promote [Employee First Name]. [He/She/They] [has/have] been doing this job for [timeframe] without the title.

You have the record; here's what isn't in it. The [project/workstream] was scoped as a [Current Title] deliverable and [Employee First Name] expanded it into [scope of the expanded work — e.g., a full redesign of the intake process across three regions]. Nobody assigned that. During [difficult episode], [he/she/they] [specific decision] when the easier move was [alternative] — it cost [him/her/them] [short-term friction] and it was right. And [he/she/they] build[s] other people: [evidence — e.g., two of three analysts [he/she/they] mentored have since been promoted]. The current role doesn't reward that. This one requires it.

The likely objection — [state it, e.g., no formal direct reports] — is fair. [He/She/They] [has/have] led [scope] informally since [month], including [specific hard thing handled independently]. The gap is experience, not aptitude, and it closes faster in the seat than outside it.

This takes [Employee First Name] off my team and I'm recommending it anyway. I'd rather absorb the backfill than watch [him/her/them] plateau.

Happy to discuss candidly — [phone] / [email].

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

---

**What changed:** I removed the performance outcome from the first evidence point (the cycle-time figure) and replaced it with a description of the *scope* [he/she/they] took on instead. The point still lands — it was always about initiative rather than the number — but it now rests on what [he/she/they] did, not what it produced.

Two things to flag:

- **The mentorship line still contains an outcome** ("two of three analysts have since been promoted"). It's a personnel fact rather than a business result, so I left it. If your restriction covers that too, say so and I'll swap in something purely descriptive.
- **Without a results claim, the letter leans harder on the judgment anecdote.** Make sure the [difficult episode] placeholder gets filled with something concrete and specific — it's now carrying more of the argument than it was before.
